item.title: When 'overcapacity' bites back, European Commission starts crying foul: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27 00:23:00
EU Illustration: Xia Qing/GT What Europe needs is strategic autonomy, not strategic dependence. It needs to confront its own problems, including high energy costs, regulatory burdens and insufficient innovation, rather than stripping the label of "overcapacity" off itself and slapping it onto others. The Office of the United States Trade Representative recently announced the results of its Section 301 investigation into "overcapacity" and released proposed measures, proposing additional Section 301 tariffs on 14 economies, including China and the EU. Although the new tariffs have not yet taken effect, their potential economic impact has already drawn widespread attention. Various parties have responded - whether firmly opposing trade protectionism or expressing a desire to seek agreements - all reflecting positions based on their own interests. But among these voices, one stands out as particularly bizarre: that of the European Commission. European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill first said that the bloc "strongly rejects" the tariff threat. However, his objection was rooted not in morality, rules, or fairness, but in self-exoneration - claiming that Europe is "among those most exposed to overcapacity." He then pointed the finger at "state-driven" overcapacity "concentrated in third countries," hinting that Europe could team up with the US for "joint action." Who the "third country" is needs no explanation. The moment Washington raised its tariff stick, the European Commission immediately waved the white flag, willingly offering itself as an accomplice in exchange for being spared. It is a truly pathetic spectacle. "Overcapacity" is itself a fabricated unilateral tool laced with strong trade-protectionist overtones; it is a complete false proposition. Certain countries, under the excuse of "overcapacity," politicize normal market competition and weaponize industrial development issues. This can only disrupt the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains as well as industrial cooperation, elevate global inflation levels, harm the vital interests of businesses and consumers, and bring long-term systemic risks to world economic growth. When the US uses this tool to target the EU, the European side should have fundamentally questioned the legitimacy of the concept itself. But the European Commission's choice was the opposite: It did not contest the accusation of "overcapacity," but only argued "I am not the source; the source is a third party" - equivalent to competing for the position of "accomplice" in the defendant's dock. Even more ironically, the EU itself was one of the early adopters of the "overcapacity" rhetoric. From the multi-year anti-subsidy investigations and duties on Chinese electric vehicles starting in 2023, to sharply cutting steel duty-free quotas in the name of "addressing overseas overcapacity" and raising out-of-quota tariffs to 50 percent, to contemplating imitating the US "Section 301" to create a "European version of 301" tool, the EU has repeatedly branded China with the label of "overcapacity," using the rhetoric as a pretext for deploying protectionist trade measures. Now that Washington has turned the very same weapon against it, the European Commission is finally crying foul. But that comes rather too late. The bigger problem is that the EU has turned the very partner it most needs to cooperate with into a bargaining chip to curry favor with the US. The more aggressively Washington wields its tariff stick, the more urgently the EU should seek to diversify its trade relationships to hedge against US policy uncertainty. China and the EU are each other's second-largest trading partners. From automobiles and new energy to biomedicine and machinery, their industrial and supply chains are deeply intertwined, their strengths complementary, and their markets highly interdependent. Yet the European Commission is seeking to secure its own security by taking a tougher stance on China. This amounts to deliberately severing external economic ties with the greatest growth potential in an attempt to shore up an already deeply fractured transatlantic alliance. With its industries in decline and its economic and trade activities constrained on all fronts, what leverage would the EU have in negotiating security with the US? One of the episodes in its history that the EU takes greatest pride in is its decision in 1998 to challenge the compliance of Section 301 of the US Trade Act at the World Trade Organization (WTO), insisting that unilateral action must be subject to multilateral authorization. Nearly three decades later, where have the European side's confidence and resolve gone? Today, unilateralism and protectionism continue to spread, putting the international economic and trade order under strain. As one of the world's largest single markets, the EU is well positioned to say "no" to unreasonable US tariffs and has every right to demand that Washington return to the framework of multilateral rules to resolve disputes. What Europe needs is strategic autonomy, not strategic dependence. It needs to confront its own problems, including high energy costs, regulatory burdens and insufficient innovation, rather than stripping the label of "overcapacity" off itself and slapping it onto others. In the manufacturing sector, global supply chains are highly interdependent; the absence of any single link will affect the overall operational efficiency. If the EU chooses to coordinate its position with China and other affected economies to jointly defend the WTO-centered multilateral trading system, it would emerge from this tariff storm with far greater dignity and security than it enjoys today.

item.title: EU reportedly shuts China out of quantum procurement; move of protectionist nature, may slow own devt: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 23:29:00
Audiences observe a superconducting quantum computer at the Digital-Intelligent Technology Ecosystem Conference 2025 in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, on December 5, 2025. Photo: VCG The EU has reportedly singled out Chinese suppliers from procurement in its freshly unveiled initiative to develop its quantum sector. Chinese analysts and industry insiders said that the move is blatant discrimination against Chinese companies and reflects a growing trend in the EU to politicize trade and economic matters. Excluding Chinese suppliers that can offer cost-effective solutions may slow the EU's quantum development, they warned. On Wednesday, the European Commission unveiled the Quantum Act, a framework aimed at converting Europe's quantum research into products and services. The act is intended to bolster European quantum research and industrial capacity, catalyze investment in public procurement while supporting European companies, the European Commission said in a post. "Given the possible impact of quantum technologies for security and the Union's strategic interests and technological autonomy, it is necessary to restrict procurement procedures to products, systems and services that are provided by Union controlled entities," the draft legislation said, per Reuters. It said entities from third countries with which the EU has a respective reciprocal partnership as well as those signed up to the World Trade Organization's general procurement agreement could also bid for tenders. As the WTO agreement on procurement does not include China, Chinese companies are set to be excluded, according to the SCMP. Chinese analysts criticized the EU plan, which they said is outright protectionist. The exclusion of Chinese companies is outright discrimination, and the EU has in recent years rolled out similar regulations that on the surface claimed to be fair and open but in reality, contained provisions that target Chinese companies, Huo Jianguo, a vice chairperson of the China Society for World Trade Organization Studies in Beijing, told the Global Times on Thursday. Quantum technology is a nascent industry that major powers have heavily invested in. Exclusive measures against Chinese companies will inevitably undercut the international cooperation essential to the sector's development. "Discrimination against Chinese firms will only hold back the EU's own progress in quantum technology," Huo said. In a statement responding to Global Times inquiry on Thursday, the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU (CCCEU) acknowledged the necessity of the EU's push to build a domestic quantum industry and secure its supply chains. The CCCEU noted, however, that the quantum technology is still at an early stage of industrialization and depends heavily on global research collaboration and division of labor along the industrial chain. As such, exclusionary procurement rules risk forming closed technological blocs and driving up the cost of innovation, the CCCEU said. It should be noted that the procurement-access arrangements currently apply only to specific public procurement covered by the act, which is still under legislative review and leaves room for further consultation, the CCCEU said. "We call on the EU to adhere to the principles of reciprocity and non-discrimination, properly balance industrial security with open cooperation, keep channels for market-oriented procurement and research exchanges between China and the EU open, avoid bloc-based fragmentation in frontier technologies, and jointly safeguard an open global innovation ecosystem." Quantum equipment from China offers advantages in terms of performance specifications and cost-effectiveness, Guo Guoping, director at the Anhui Quantum Computing Engineering Research Center, told the Global Times on Thursday. "The EU is not a monolithic bloc, so while Chinese firms might miss out on certain government incentives within the EU, they can still compete effectively by offering high-quality, affordably priced products, much like the case with new-energy vehicles," the expert said. In the long term, Chinese quantum computing companies should prioritize independent, self-reliant technological development. They should also focus on fostering cooperation, exchange and ecosystem-building with countries in the Global South, Guo said. It is essential to fully leverage China's comprehensive industrial supply chain, manufacturing capabilities, and cost advantages, while also tapping into the vast user bases and markets found both within China and across the Global South, noted Guo. The EU is home to 32 percent of the world's quantum companies, higher than 25 percent in the US and 5 percent in China. It trails, however, in terms of quantum patents, with the bloc accounting for just 6 percent compared with 23 percent in the US and 46 percent in China, according to a report last year from the EC. Since the beginning of this year, the EU has introduced revisions to the Cybersecurity Act, the Industrial Accelerator Act and the Public Procurement Act. Under the pretexts of cybersecurity and industrial development, the bloc is pursuing protectionism by repeatedly introducing discriminatory provisions and continuously tightening market access conditions, He Yadong, a spokesperson of China's Ministry of Commerce, said on September 17. China urges the EU to abide by WTO rules, keep its market open, revise these discriminatory provisions in the proposed legislation, and create a fair, transparent and non-discriminatory business environment for companies investing and operating in the EU, He said.

item.title: Pakistani minister praises Chinese public's warm send-off for Shenzhou-24 crew, China's willingness to share its success
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 23:21:00
Pakistani minister praises Chinese public's warm send-off for Shenzhou-24 crew, China's willingness to share its success By Dong Feng and Li Yu Published: Nov 26, 2026 11:21 PM Updated: Nov 26, 2026 11:33 PM Professor Ahsan Iqbal (left), Pakistan's Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives, speaks at a media talk in the Pakistan Embassy in Beijing, on November 26, 2026. Photo: Dong Feng / Global Times Following China's successful launch of the Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft on Wednesday, sending three astronauts, including a Pakistani astronaut, into the orbiting Tiangong space station, Pakistan's Federal Minister for Planning, Development & Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal spoke at a media event on Thursday where he highlighted the warm farewell for the departing astronauts, and the enthusiastic cheers from the Chinese people for the Pakistani astronaut at the send-off ceremony, and a distinctive feature of China's development policy: its willingness to share its success with other countries. Iqbal said the scientific experiments to be conducted by Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali aboard China's Tiangong space station could help Pakistan address food security challenges. The research would provide Pakistani scientists with insights into developing smart agriculture and weather-resistant seed varieties, while materials science experiments could also help strengthen the country's industrial capabilities. He said collaboration with China and future satellite launches could also strengthen Pakistan's satellite navigation capabilities, with applications in water management, agriculture, urban planning, logistics and connectivity. More than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests are planned for the Shenzhou-24 mission, covering space life sciences, space material science, microgravity fluid physics and combustion science, fundamental physics, space medicine and new space technologies, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). Four China-Pakistan cooperative projects in the fields of biotechnology and materials will be conducted during the Shenzhou-24 mission, and the Pakistani payload specialist Ali will conduct an experiment on photosynthetic cyanobacteria, which was proposed by the Pakistan Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), the Xinhua News Agency reported. Iqbal said space technology had become an integral part of national development planning, warning that countries that failed to acquire emerging technologies would struggle to compete in the future. He described cooperation with China as timely, saying it would provide Pakistan with critical knowledge and capabilities to harness new technologies for the benefit of its people. Iqbal described the mission as another flagship project of Pakistan-China cooperation, extending a partnership built through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) on the ground into space. China-Pakistan space cooperation spans more than three decades. In 1990, Pakistan's first experimental satellite, Badr-1, was launched aboard a Chinese rocket from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center. More recently, China launched Pakistan's cube satellite aboard the Chang'e-6 probe in 2024 and placed a Pakistani remote-sensing satellite in orbit via a Long March-6 rocket in April 2026, according to Xinhua. Looking beyond space cooperation, Iqbal said Pakistan and China were discussing the need for a knowledge corridor to prepare Pakistan's younger generation for emerging technologies. He said the government's Uraan Pakistan agenda placed a high priority on equipping young people with the skills and knowledge needed for Industrial Revolutions 4.0 and 5.0. Pakistan's National Economic Transformation Plan 2024-29, known as Uraan Pakistan, focuses on exports, equity and empowerment, environment, food and water security, energy and infrastructure, while the country's government will focus on growing industry, commerce and information technology, according to Xinhua. Pakistan hopes to have at least 10,000 PhD students receive training at top Chinese universities over the next 10 years in fields including artificial intelligence, space sciences, materials science, biotechnology, big data, automation and robotics, Iqbal said. The initiative aims to prepare a new generation of researchers, scientists and leaders who can drive Pakistan's future development. Answering a question from the Global Times about the alignment between China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) and Pakistan's development agenda, Iqbal said the two were well aligned. Under the second phase of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, known as CPEC 2.0, Pakistan had identified five cooperation corridors: growth, livelihoods, innovation, green economy and openness to broader regional cooperation. Iqbal also cited space exploration as an example of advanced-science cooperation, noting that an agreement signed in February 2025 had been put into practice through the participation of a Pakistani astronaut in the Shenzhou-24 mission in November 2026. He said Pakistan hoped to further cooperate with China in space exploration, including drawing on China's planned crewed lunar landing before 2030 as Pakistan works toward its own lunar landing goal by 2035. "I think that is the uniqueness of China's policy of development, that it is willing to share its successes with other countries," Iqbal said, recalling his experience at the send-off ceremony, the warmth and the affection that Chinese people expressed when saying goodbye to the departing astronauts. Iqbal said what really impressed him was that thousands of Chinese people had gathered to farewell to the astronauts. "So that really reflected the special bond between China and Pakistan, not just at the government level, but also at the people-to-people level... Every media channel has covered it [the Shenzhou-24 mission] from East to West, and everyone is talking about it and appreciating China's commitment toward sharing its successes with the developing countries and Global South, and particularly with Pakistan. And this opens a new avenue of collaboration between Global South and China in many fields," Iqbal said.

item.title: China unveils 5-year services trade plan to widen market access, advance high-level opening-up despite global complexity
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 23:18:00
Tourists from Vietnam pose for selfies in Kunming, southwest China's Yunnan Province, May 2, 2026. China's inbound tourism booms thanks to visa exemption policies. (Photo by Hao Yaxin/Xinhua) China on Thursday unveiled a five-year plan for the development of trade in services, outlining measures to further integrate its services sector into the global economy, a move that a Chinese expert said sends a clear signal of the country's continued commitment to high-level opening-up. At a time when rising protectionism and trade barriers are weighing on global business confidence, China's continued efforts to expand market access and facilitate the cross-border flows of data, capital and personnel stand in contrast to the growing trend of trade restrictions in some economies, the expert said. The plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, jointly released by eight departments, including the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM), the Publicity Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, outlines 25 key tasks across seven areas. By 2030, China aims to steadily expand its services trade, including further increasing its share of the country's total foreign trade, achieving more balanced imports and exports, and significantly enhancing its international competitiveness, according to the plan. China is already a large and growing market for foreign services providers. According to figures included in the plan, China's total services trade exceeded 8 trillion yuan for the first time in 2025, reaching 8.08 trillion yuan and accounting for 15.1 percent of the country's total foreign trade. Services imports reached 4.46 trillion yuan, recording an average annual growth rate of 11.1 percent during the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-25) period. To better meet the country's growing demand for high-quality services, China will steadily expand market access in key sectors, including value-added telecommunications and healthcare, to attract more internationally renowned enterprises to invest in China and introduce a wider range of services into the domestic market, according to the plan. The country will also revise and release its catalog of encouraged services imports, expanding imports of research and development, design, resource recycling and environmental management services, while encouraging imports of high-quality consumer services in areas such as healthcare, the performing arts and sporting events. "China's industrial upgrading and evolving consumption needs are generating demand for increasingly sophisticated services... This presents considerable opportunities for international services providers, particularly in areas where they possess established technological or professional expertise," Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times. In addition to further implementing its negative list for cross-border trade in services and advancing comprehensive pilot and demonstration programs for expanding opening-up in the services sector, China has also vowed to introduce measures to facilitate the cross-border business activities of multinational companies. For example, the plan announced on Thursday supports eligible regions in exploring arrangements to facilitate the cross-border transfer of personal information within multinational companies. It also calls for more efficient security assessments for outbound transfers of important data and personal information, which would facilitate compliant cross-border data transfers by enterprises and institutions engaged in services trade. The document also supports eligible enterprises in operating integrated domestic and foreign currency cash pools to facilitate intragroup fund allocation, and calls for greater convenience in cross-border travel for foreign nationals, including executives and technical personnel. China's efforts to reduce institutional barriers to cross-border business activities also extend to closer alignment with international economic and trade rules. According to the plan, China will take the lead in pilot programs for the implementation of the World Trade Organization agreements on electronic commerce and investment facilitation, while actively pursuing negotiations in services trade and investment. Notably, alongside these efforts to improve regulatory compatibility, the plan explicitly calls for strengthening policy dialogue and mutually beneficial cooperation with major economies such as the US and the EU in services trade sectors including tourism, finance and insurance, telecommunications and the computer sector, cloud operations and creative design. All these areas of cooperation highlight an often overlooked aspect of China's economic relations with developed economies, said Hu, since much of the trade imbalance debate in the West has focused on merchandise trade, while economies such as the US have long maintained substantial services trade surpluses with China. According to the Office of the US Trade Representative, the US services trade surplus with China stood at $34.4 billion in 2025, up 6.9 percent compared with 2024. China's efforts to further expand services imports despite its existing services trade deficit reflect its commitment to promoting more balanced trade, in line with its stated position that "it does not pursue trade surpluses," Li Changan, a professor at the Academy of China Open Economy Studies at the University of International Business and Economics, told the Global Times. By further opening its growing services market and improving the business environment, China is turning domestic demand into commercial opportunities for its trading partners worldwide, particularly valuable as rising trade barriers constrain global growth, said Li.

item.title: GT Voice: India's construction equipment localization drive should not be trapped in an anti-China narrative
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 22:28:00
China-India industrial cooperation potential Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT India's Union Cabinet has approved an eight-year industrial support program with a total outlay of 110 billion rupees ($1.19 billion). The initiative aims to improve the country's manufacturing of construction and infrastructure equipment (CIE) and its components, as well as establish a dedicated CIE testing facility, thereby enhancing self-reliance and positioning India as a key player in the global CIE market. However, some Indian media outlets have linked this industrial support policy to claimed concerns over the supply of Chinese equipment. The Economic Times said that the move comes amid "China's restrictions on exports of certain heavy equipment, including tunnel boring machines." India's business news channel CNBC TV18 interpreted the plan as "part of the government's broader push to build domestic manufacturing capacity and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers." It added that India largely depends on China for these machines, which are used in infrastructure projects in hilly, high-altitude and border areas. India's development of its construction equipment industry has its own economic logic, and there is no need to link a normal process of industrialization to a "de-China" or an "anti-China" narrative. According to some media reports, approval of the plan followed nearly two years of discussions between the construction equipment industry and the government on financial incentives to boost domestic manufacturing. This shows that the industry's underlying economic rationale long predates recent supply concerns. As a developing economy undergoing rapid industrialization and urbanization, India's desire to build a domestic construction equipment industry is not hard to understand. As construction of roads, railways, ports and other infrastructure continues, demand for construction equipment in India keeps growing. India is the world's third-largest market for CIE, after China and the US. Indian government figures put the market at about 975 billion rupees ($11 billion) in fiscal year 2024-25. Fueled by rapid growth in infrastructure and housing, it is projected to more than double to roughly 2.28 trillion rupees by fiscal 2029-30. This vast market demand provides a practical foundation for nurturing indigenous manufacturing capacity. China has no reason to see India's industrial progress as a threat. What truly warrants caution is that some Indian manufacturers are trying to secure more market space for local production by imposing tariffs and tightening local sourcing requirements. High-end construction equipment is technology-, capital- and supply-chain-intensive. Its production involves precision machinery, hydraulic systems, core components, industrial controls and many other components. Erecting trade barriers while India's supporting industrial base is still immature may drive up equipment procurement and production costs, potentially slowing the country's ambitious infrastructure build-out. The concerns expressed by multinational manufacturers operating in India deserve to be taken seriously. How to turn vast domestic market demand into a competitive edge for local manufacturing is a challenge shared by many developing countries still undergoing industrialization. China's CIE also went through a stage when its technological foundations were weak and it relied heavily on imported core components. The path it took to upgrade could offer useful lessons for India. Looking back at the development of China's CIE, opening-up and cooperation, on the one hand, and independent innovation, on the other, have always been two mutually reinforcing main threads. In the 1980s, Chinese construction equipment companies introduced advanced foreign technologies on a large scale. Take Chinese leading construction equipment maker company LiuGong as an example. The company introduced technology from US-based Caterpillar in 1987 and formed a joint venture with Germany's ZF Friedrichshafen AG in 1995. It then steadily strengthened its research and development (R&D) efforts and gradually built an industrial system covering complete machines, core components and services. In recent years, Chinese construction equipment companies have made breakthroughs in electrification, intelligent technologies and other fields. This development path shows that international cooperation does not necessarily lead to technological dependence, and that opening markets does not mean giving up independent innovation. The key lies in whether international technologies and industrial resources can be effectively combined with a country's own R&D capabilities, market demand and engineering practice, so that external resources become endogenous drivers of development. As the global construction equipment industry accelerates its shift toward intelligent and green technologies, China and India still have broad room for cooperation in equipment manufacturing, component supply, technology R&D and other areas. Some Indian manufacturers need to realize that China's mature construction equipment industrial chain is not an obstacle to India's localization drive, but rather an important resource that can help India shorten its industrial upgrading cycle and improve manufacturing efficiency. How to cultivate independent innovation capacities through opening-up and cooperation is an important question for India's construction equipment industry as it moves toward global competition. For India, the yardstick for manufacturing success should not be merely how much its import dependence has fallen, but whether its companies can build sustainable technological advantages and competitiveness in the international market. Self-reliance does not mean self-isolation, and localization should not become synonymous with protectionism.

item.title: How the US uses chip curbs, investment screening, entity listings and security rhetoric to target China's tech advances; moves doomed to fail: experts
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 22:27:00
Razor wire at the US Capitol Photo: VCG Democrats have vowed to launch sweeping investigations into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the company and the Trump administration following Huang's reinstatement, opening a new front in Washington's increasingly contentious debate over how access to advanced AI chips is regulated. Huang's return to Nvidia is unlikely to mark the end of the controversy. Instead, it could signal the beginning of another round of political and policy battles over China's access to advanced computing technology, analysts said. Some lawmakers who oppose his reinstatement may use the controversy to push for tighter chip export controls, potentially bringing China hawks from both parties closer together on restricting China's technological development. It is noteworthy that Republicans and Democrats may differ over the methods and political tactics they employ, but they share a broader objective of maintaining US technological superiority and limiting China's progress in advanced AI, according to experts. The Huang episode is far from an isolated incident. The Global Times found that Washington has been deploying a broader set of measures, ranging from chip and computing-power restrictions to investment screening, entity-list designations and narratives portraying China's technological advances as so-called "security threats." What lies behind this multi-pronged strategy? And how far is Washington prepared to go to slow China's technological rise? Foreign visitors learn about new robots at the 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing on August 19, 2026. Photo: VCG From chip restrictions to broader legislative push House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become House speaker when the new Congress convenes, and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer have strongly opposed Huang's reinstatement, vowing to launch a wide-ranging investigation into Nvidia. He Weiwen, a senior fellow at the Center for China and Globalization, told the Global Times that the congressional investigation may target Nvidia and Huang personally, focusing on whether the company's China dealings violated US export control laws and whether commercial interests created substantive "national security" risks. Meanwhile, it may also target the Trump administration, focusing on whether the White House broke congressional law in clearing the way for Nvidia, and if so, what motivated it and whether officials' personal financial interests were involved. "This track goes directly to the legitimacy and political responsibility of the executive branch," He noted. The investigation could last months or even years, and its impact will extend beyond any legal conclusion: it will further deteriorate the overall environment for US high-tech exports abroad, especially to China, the expert said. Meanwhile, lawmakers from both parties are seeking to write tougher export controls into law, making restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips more difficult for future administrations to reverse. For instance, Republican Senator Tom Cotton has urged Congress to pass the Chip Security Act, which would require chipmakers to track the locations of advanced AI processors and notify the government if they suspect that chips have reached prohibited users. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has argued that Huang's return makes it more urgent to codify bipartisan export control measures into law. Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, meanwhile, has backed the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act. The bill seeks to pressure US allies to tighten restrictions on advanced chipmaking equipment supplied to China, or face potential unilateral US restrictions. Their convergence suggests that the debate surrounding Huang's reinstatement could provide fresh momentum for a broader, bipartisan effort to tighten controls on China's access to advanced technology. China has consistently opposed any practice of overstretching the concept of national security and abusing export controls. "Should the relevant bills be enacted into law, they would severely undermine the international economic and trade order and disrupt the stability of the global semiconductor industrial and supply chains," warned the Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson. A protester displays a banner reading "China Is Not Our Enemy" during the first hearing of the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the US and China on February 28, 2023. Photo: VCG Expanding campaign on AI models "China's sci-tech progress relies on independent innovation and open cooperation," China's Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning stressed at a regular press conference on November 12. In reality, beyond chips and computing power, Washington is also extending its restrictions to the use and procurement of Chinese AI models. On October 19, the US Department of Homeland Security required the agencies to remove DeepSeek products as well as third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek from their IT systems, according to a notice made public. On the same day, the US government expanded its use of sanctions against Chinese technology-related entities under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act. The action is seen as a sign of Washington's growing willingness to use intellectual property protection and sanctions to target entities connected to China's emerging technology sector. Washington has also increasingly framed competition over AI models as a "national security" issue. On September 8, the NSA, FBI and CISA jointly issued a cybersecurity advisory accusing China-based AI companies of conducting industrial-scale knowledge distillation campaigns to extract proprietary capabilities from US frontier models. The advisory acknowledged that knowledge distillation is a legitimate and widely used AI development technique, but it still alleged that some Chinese companies were using it on an industrial scale to obtain restricted capabilities from US models. Chinese analysts pointed out that Washington has sought to turn competition over model capabilities into another front in its broader "national security" campaign against China's AI industry. At the congressional level, Chinese AI and robotics companies have also increasingly become subjects of scrutiny. Chinese industry insiders slammed Washington's hegemonic bullying of Chinese artificial intelligence firms, saying its claims lack factual basis and risk fueling confrontation and mistrust in the AI sector, undermining the industry's development. Besides, Washington is also seeking to coordinate with allies to build a more tightly aligned technology supply chain. On November 15, the US and nine other governments signed the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity at the Pax Silica Founders Retreat in San Francisco. Although the declaration does not explicitly establish a China-specific export-control alliance, its emphasis on trusted technology partnerships, supply-chain diversification and reducing strategic dependencies has broader implications for global technology competition. Beyond formal restrictions, Washington is also seeking to shape international perceptions of Chinese AI through public narratives via media tools. Some US policymakers and commentators have increasingly framed Chinese open-source models in terms of security, ideological influence and potential vulnerabilities. Wang Shouyang, a distinguished research fellow at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told the Global Times in a previous interview that the US is trying to use a "chilling effect" in its competition with China in AI - leveraging public opinion and cognitive influence to create an environment in which companies in the US and around the world "dare not use, do not want to use and cannot publicly use" Chinese open-source models. For example, the US media outlet Axios, citing sources' opinions, reported on July 20 that "instead of a ban, another source familiar with government discussions described a push to highlight potential backdoors and lack of security with Chinese models, and the governance issue that brings." It added that while such measures do not amount to an outright ban, they "would have a chilling effect on Chinese open-source tech and US companies that rely on it." Containment strategies a 'dead end' He Weiwen noted that partisan maneuvering and the China-focused "national security" narrative continue to advance in parallel. "Throughout the power struggle among the White House, Congress, and Silicon Valley, China remains the predetermined target. From scrutinizing companies' normal commercial ties with the Chinese market to tightening chip export controls against China, US political circles consistently fold their protectionist policies into a 'national security' narrative," He said, noting that China has never intervened in this internal American dispute, yet it has been forced to serve as the backdrop for every accusation. "The fundamental aim of the US' crackdown on China's tech industry is to severely hold back the country's technological development and keep it permanently lagging behind the US. Looking at the actual results of the tech war so far, however, this goal has not been achieved," Xiang Ligang, director-general of the Zhongguancun Modern Information Consumer Application Industry Technology Alliance, told the Global Times. Xiang said that China's relevant tech industries continue to develop normally. Businesses in telecommunications, artificial intelligence, computing, PCs, smartphones and even smart vehicles are all still advancing steadily. "The US pressure has in fact had the opposite effect: it has spurred China's technological development and stimulated greater investment and progress in high-tech fields," he stressed. For example, the US has blocked China's access to EUV lithography machines, aiming to lock down its ability to iterate on advanced process nodes. Yet Chinese tech giant Huawei has released the Kirin 9050 Pro - the first chip to implement Tau Scaling Law and LogicFolding technologies - shifting from reliance on new lithography processes to a fundamental redesign at the architectural level. Moreover, despite the continued tightening of US advanced computing export controls on China, DeepSeek's innovations in Mixture-of-Experts and Multi-head Latent Attention broke the equation that "compute blockade equals capability blockade." These advances helped maintain the competitiveness of China's AI models, while the company's open-source strategy further accelerated global progress in artificial intelligence. From chips and operating systems to industrial software, every supply cutoff has forced the accelerated emergence of an independent technological pathway, and every attempt to choke off access has driven the industrial chain to turn its weaknesses into a priority list of key research challenges. He Weiwen noted that Washington needs to wake up from the outdated Cold War mindset of the 1950s, break free from its obsession with zero-sum games, stop arbitrarily wielding the "national security" stick to stigmatize and contain China's tech industry, and return to the path of mutually beneficial cooperation in the semiconductor and AI sectors between China and the US. "Political maneuvering that insists on fabricating imaginary enemies is a dead end," he said.

item.title: China-India border situation 'remains generally stable'; expert says dialogue a shared understanding to help prevent escalation of friction
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 21:50:00
Chen Xi, spokesperson for China's Ministry of National Defense The situation in the China-India border areas remains generally stable, a Chinese Ministry of National Defense spokesperson said at a press conference on Thursday. Chen Xi, spokesperson for the ministry, stressed that the Zangnan region is China's territory and that China does not recognize the so-called "Arunachal Pradesh" illegally set up by India. China and India maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels, including general-level talks, to jointly implement the consensus reached by the two sides and safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas. He made the remarks when asked about reports that Chinese and Indian military officials held high-level talks this month in the so-called "Arunachal Pradesh" (China's Zangnan), with border management among the key topics. Chen's remarks came a day after the Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson said at a media briefing on Wednesday that a meeting of the senior military commanders was held in the eastern sector recently. Discussions between the two sides focused on improving border management as well as addressing outstanding issues along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Indian Express reported. The ministry's spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that "India and China engage regularly through diplomatic and military mechanisms" when responding to questions. Jaiswal also said that such interactions are aimed at maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas and preventing any escalation, per the Indian Express report. The recent statements by China and India on senior military commander-level talks in the eastern sector, coupled with China's reaffirmation of its sovereignty over the Zangnan region, send a clear signal that China's position on territorial sovereignty remains firm, while maintaining stability through dialogue remains a shared understanding between the two sides, Qian Feng, director of the Research Department at Tsinghua University's National Strategy Institute, told the Global Times on Thursday. The two sides have continued to communicate through military and diplomatic channels to prevent local friction from escalating, using existing meeting mechanisms as a pressure valve to ease tensions, Qian said. China and India agreed at the 25th round of talks between their Special Representatives on the boundary question in Beijing on August 25 to strengthen border management mechanisms, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. Strengthening border management mechanisms was among the outcomes of the 25th round of talks between the Special Representatives of China and India on the boundary question, held in Beijing on August 25. The two sides reached eight points of outcomes and consensus including agreements to address situations on the ground through existing diplomatic and military channels, resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstandings and miscalculations along the LAC. The two sides also agreed to add two meeting points for general-level talks and establish two additional border military hotlines in the eastern and middle sectors, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. On October 26, responding to Indian claims that Chinese forces had diverged from established patrolling patterns, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China strictly abides by the relevant agreements and common understandings reached between the two countries, and conducts normal border patrol and control activities to safeguard its territorial sovereignty and stability in the border areas. China and India maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels. We hope that India will work with China in the same direction by jointly implementing the common understandings reached between the two sides and maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas with concrete actions.

item.title: World's first Tibetan-language search engine marks 10th anniversary with 1.3 million daily visits on average
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 21:42:00
Tourists pose for photos at Potala Palace square in Lhasa, Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on October 15, as the 2026 "Winter Tour in Xizang" campaign launches. From October 15, 2026 to March 15, 2027, all A-level scenic spots in Xizang (except temple sites) are open to visitors free of charge. Photo: CNS Photo Yongzin.com, the world's first Tibetan-language search engine, now records an average of 1.3 million visits per day as it marked its 10th launch anniversary. The search engine serves users across all 34 provincial-level regions in China and 96 countries and regions worldwide, including the US, France, Japan, Russia and Singapore, China News Service reported on Thursday. Serving as a unified gateway to major Tibetan-language websites across China, a major source of Tibetan-language information on the internet and a resource-sharing hub, yongzin.com has evolved into a comprehensive Tibetan-language online system built around information sharing and search services. The system integrates a Tibetan-language search engine, multi-platform applications, an automatic Tibetan word-segmentation and intelligent language analysis system, and a high-efficiency web crawler. Over the past decade, the platform has undergone continuous upgrades, addressing gaps in the supply of Tibetan-language online information while expanding its range of services. Initially offering searches for webpages, news, images, audio and video, it has gradually expanded to include a Tibetan-language encyclopedia, document library and question-and-answer system. It has also launched supporting products such as a mobile app and a Tibetan-Chinese (Putonghua)-English input tool, with total mobile downloads exceeding 3 million. At present, the platform's document library contains more than 90,000 volumes and articles of Tibetan ancient texts, academic literature and folk writings. Its collections cover more than 30 fields, including politics, economics, history, literature, Tibetan medicine and natural sciences. The recently launched version 3.0 of the search engine has undergone a complete overhaul of its underlying architecture. It introduces four new modules including Tibetan optical character recognition (OCR), bidirectional Chinese-Tibetan machine translation, Tibetan academic search and a Tibetan calligraphy section. It also integrates Tibetan-language voice search, with speech recognition accuracy exceeding 92 percent. In addition, the bidirectional Chinese-Tibetan machine translation module, powered by a large AI model, can accurately translate Chinese-language documents into Tibetan, making information more accessible to grass-roots rural and pastoral communities. The Tibetan academic search function overcomes the limitations of the previous version, which only supported title searches, by enabling advanced searches by author, keywords and full text, filling a gap in specialized Tibetan-language academic search services. The newly launched Tibetan calligraphy section also enriches the digital presentation of the Tibetan ethnic culture. According to the platform's development plan, the yongzin.com platform will complete the integration of its speech synthesis function by the end of this year, adding audio playback to help users access news reports and classical texts. item.title: Beyond bloc rivalry: China-Cambodia 'Golden Dragon' drills offer an alternative security model
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 19:38:00
Chinese soldiers participate in the opening of a joint exercise involving the Chinese and Cambodian militaries at a Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center at Port Ream, Cambodia on Nov. 25, 2026. The Chinese and Cambodian militaries have launched a joint exercise in Cambodia on Wednesday. Photo: Xinhua The China-Cambodia "Golden Dragon" joint exercise takes place almost every year, yet some Western media outlets continue to recycle the same narrative in their coverage. On Wednesday, China and Cambodia launched the largest edition of the exercise to date. An Associated Press report portrayed the exercise as part of China's efforts to expand its regional influence and once again cited the US' ongoing "concerns" about China-Cambodia military cooperation. It also highlighted the expansion of Cambodia's Ream Naval Base with Chinese funding on the southern coast, claiming that the facility "could become a strategic outpost for the Chinese navy in the Gulf of Thailand." In fact, launched in 2016, the "Golden Dragon" exercises have now entered their eighth edition and evolved into a regular and institutionalized platform for regional security cooperation. The publicly announced scenarios for the exercises focus on counter-terrorism, counter-piracy, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief. Military attachés from multiple countries were invited as on-site observers, and both China and Cambodia have repeatedly stressed that the exercises are not directed against any third party. However, whenever China and Cambodia stage the "Golden Dragon" exercises, many Western media outlets overlook the actual objectives of the exercises and cast them through the lens of great-power rivalry. In fact, China-Cambodia drills are fundamentally different from US-led exercises across Southeast Asia. Current-affairs commentator Song Zhongping noted that "Golden Dragon" focuses on non-traditional security and non-combat military operations, without a designated adversary. By contrast, US-led drills in Southeast Asia center on traditional security and wartime scenarios. They deploy a wide array of weaponry and are designed around clearly identified hypothetical adversaries and potential third-party contingencies. The US-Philippines "Balikatan" exercises offer a case in point. They regularly involve more than 10,000 troops, with participation reaching approximately 17,000 in 2024. The exercises are explicitly framed around the need to "respond to regional threats." The two categories of drills differ at their core. The facts about the much-discussed Ream Naval Base are straightforward. Song Zhongping stresses first that Ream Naval Base is fully Cambodian-owned and operated, and China has not leased the facility, which is fundamentally different from US overseas military bases. According to Song, Chinese naval vessels make temporary port calls there for two main purposes. First, to support the training of Cambodian naval personnel and deliver military and naval-equipment assistance. Second, to meet the routine logistical needs of Chinese vessels, including resupply and crew rest, while supporting maritime security in the Strait of Malacca and carrying out related training missions. "The Ream Naval Base is not intended for military confrontation; it is a facility to support training and capacity-building for Cambodia," he said. By comparison, US overseas bases are frequently established with specific third-country contingencies in mind. Song said that when a host-nation base is leveraged to confront another power, the installation itself becomes a geopolitical target. The host state gets dragged into conflict, threatening regional peace and stability while exposing the host country to unnecessary risks. Describing the Ream Naval Base as "a strategic outpost of the Chinese Navy" goes beyond what the facts support. A fundamental flaw in some Western commentary is the assumption that all defense cooperation between China and its neighbors is a tool for geopolitical confrontation. However, Southeast Asian countries have diverse security needs. They need partners to work together to tackle natural disasters and terrorism, rather than being forced to choose sides. Song believes that the China-Cambodia defense cooperation model offers a model that could be adapted and applied more widely across Southeast Asia. Humanitarian relief, counter-terrorism, anti-piracy and disaster-risk reduction are common challenges facing countries across the region. By sharing its practical experience and providing appropriate technology and equipment, China aims to help regional countries strengthen their capacity to carry out non-combat military operations. For Southeast Asia, this provides tangible benefits without threatening other countries. "China's participation in the construction of training and support facilities contributes to stability in the host country and across the wider region, producing mutual benefits by strengthening governance and institutional capacity," Song said. China-Cambodia defense cooperation offers an alternative model to alliance-style military blocs - one built on equal partnership, voluntary participation, a focus on shared security challenges, and a commitment to avoiding confrontation and targeting no third party. Alliance-driven drills strap partners to a war chariot, while partnership-based cooperation hands neighbors a ladder for development. Regional security is not about choosing sides; it's about teaming up. That may well be what Southeast Asia needs most.

item.title: AI face blending makes it harder to trace unauthorized use, expert warns
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 22:33:00
Photo: VCG A short video featuring a character who bears a striking resemblance to Chinese actor Peng Yuchang, in both appearance and voice, has recently sparked online discussions about AI face-blending technology. Peng's studio has also issued a statement alleging that his facial features have been used without authorization in AI training and face-blending content and calling on those responsible to stop infringement. "AI face blending is a form of generative deep synthesis, and its technical approach is fundamentally different from that of replacement-based face swapping," Yang Jinwei, head of the AI Authenticity Verification Department at Beijing RealAI Intelligent Technology Co, told the media. In traditional AI face swapping, the process begins with a source face and a target face. Facial landmarks are aligned and the poses normalized, after which the source face's texture is mapped onto and rendered over the target person's head. Essentially, it is a process of replacement, with a clearly identifiable source image, according to Capital News, a news platform operated by the Beijing Daily Group. Face blending, by contrast, relies on a facial feature encoder to convert faces into high-dimensional latent vectors. These vectors encode identity-related information, including facial contours, the arrangement of facial features, the distance between the eyebrows and eyes, nose and lip characteristics, skin tone and texture, and habitual expressions. The system then combines multiple facial vectors through weighted interpolation and feature blending before feeding them into a diffusion model or generative adversarial network to render an entirely new face image, according to Capital News. "Creators can either import multiple face images and adjust the weights assigned to different features, or use text prompts and parameter settings to define characteristics such as face shape, facial features, age and expression," Yang said. "Some creators of infringing content seek to retain enough resemblance for viewers to recognize the public figure being imitated, while altering facial details to evade automated detection tools that platforms use to compare images against original photos," he noted. Lower technical barriers have also reduced the cost of using other people's facial and vocal features without permission. Feng Anrong, a screenwriter, director and head of an AI production team, told the Global Times that some producers of low-cost, high-volume short dramas seek to maximize profits through unauthorized AI face swapping and voice cloning. "Many low-cost, high-volume productions essentially operate like commercial in-feed advertisements, relying on unauthorized AI face blending and voice cloning to reduce production costs," Feng said. "Such productions are often made in bulk and promoted by paying for increased traffic. Rather than relying on the revenue-sharing model used by traditional short-drama platforms, they may therefore fall outside conventional content review mechanisms." The large-scale production and distribution of such content also pose challenges for platforms seeking to identify and remove infringing material. Zhang Peng, a cultural studies researcher at Nanjing Normal University, told the Global Times that such content may evade some basic automated detection systems, but this does not mean it cannot be identified or that it leaves no traces. "AI technology has lowered the cost and technical barriers to replicating people's facial and vocal characteristics. Meanwhile, technical limitations in platform moderation and the high costs individuals face when pursuing legal remedies make it difficult to promptly curb infringing content," Zhang said. "For platforms, detection needs to move beyond simply comparing images and also examine facial features, the origins of generated content and whether the necessary authorization was obtained." Zhang suggested that platforms improve the traceability of AI-generated content through measures such as digital watermarking, content-tracing technologies and databases of authorized uses, while also strengthening content moderation and complaint-handling mechanisms. As AI-generated appearances do not need to be an exact match for the people being imitated, determining whether a person's rights have been infringed has become an important issue in legal practice. Li Yunkai, an intellectual property lawyer at the Beijing Tian Yuan Law Firm, told the Global Times that the key to determining whether an AI-generated image infringes a person's portrait rights is not whether it looks exactly like the individual, but whether ordinary members of the public can identify the person. "Comments under videos and discussions on social media platforms may also serve as reference points when assessing whether an individual is identifiable," Li said. "If generated content places an identifiable person in vulgar scenarios, falsely portrays them as endorsing a product, or associates them with negative stories, it may also infringe their reputation rights, and those distributing the content may bear corresponding liability."
